headings.title: Converting a queued task into steering

html:
Conversation task admission and coordination

The server accepts a conversation task once, stores its execution intent and advances it without requiring an open browser. The conversation coordinator connects composer input, task-lane ownership, native execution and UI projections. It does not treat a browser's observed capacity or a completed transport trace as permission to start another attempt.

This is the durable task path behind /api/agent/conversation-tasks. Prepared requests own a separate prepare/claim API. Follow-up queues attach future instructions to one existing task lineage and are advanced by this same coordinator.

The browser queue guide traces provisional cards, uncertain POST retries, canonical snapshot reads and explicit dependency selection at the client boundary.

Ownership and lifecycle

Owner Responsibility
ConversationTaskInput Validate submitted prompt, retry identity, dependencies, target and optional composer/policy settings.
DurableTaskQueueWorker Accept/replay intent, reconcile attempts, reserve eligible work and deliver pending steering.
Task lanes and RAM lanes Own task/submission identities, ordering, dependency checks, lane versions and attempt reservations.
Native RunStore Supply run identity, accepted state, input-state checks, ownership and steering receipts.
Composer profiles Validate visible composer intent and commit accepted profile/default changes with task admission.
Application lifecycle Start the watcher after recovery and stop it during shutdown.

Construction registers a scheduler wake signal and creates a submission pool with eight workers. That pool bounds concurrent dispatch preparation; it is not the configured model-execution capacity. The watcher waits up to one second between passes and can be woken by state changes. It catches pass-level failures, logs them and continues on later passes.

Shutdown sets the stop flag, wakes and joins the watcher for a bounded interval, then cancels pending pool futures without waiting for running submissions. Accepted tasks and external effects retain their own shutdown/recovery contracts.

Admission and exact retries

The request requires a client submission ID, prompt and Gateway ID. Prompts allow 1–24,000 characters; whitespace-only prompts and leading slash commands are rejected. At most 16 attachment references can be submitted. The lane store permits at most 32 queued tasks in one conversation. These limits are distinct from active execution capacity.

The coordinator validates agreement between visible composer values and explicit request fields. Advanced prompt overrides retain their defined precedence over composer defaults. A new conversation can carry initial permission/capability and composer defaults; existing conversation defaults use their dedicated editors. Context IDs must have the accepted form and acquire their grants through the context owner. Browser labels/locality do not select execution authority.

A deterministic digest binds the submitted intent, resolved behavior preset, accepted capability authority and any plan/direct-request identity to client_submission_id. All captured settings are not necessarily digest inputs: the saved task context separately carries supported execution settings. Exact replay returns the existing task; changed identity inputs conflict, and a consumed submission cannot silently create a replacement task. Compatibility handling keeps older default-collaboration, inherited-thinking and carry-forward retry identities readable without changing the meaning of a newly chosen option.

Accepted context includes model configuration/routing, output/Task Contract controls, redaction, context-reading and scheduling policies, target selection, parameter snapshots and supported runtime guards. require_current_snapshot requires the declared keys before publication and dispatch, and validates captured capability authority when present. It does not replace each field's own validator. Retries reuse saved values for the covered settings instead of recapturing them.

Permission intent preserves inheritance: native_permission_policy = null means no explicit prompt override. It is not a frozen copy of the current effective global/conversation policy. Later permission resolution and steering checks still consult the authority. Likewise, model Recommended-profile resolution for the selected task model happens at dispatch before its output reservation is pinned.

Publication boundaries

flowchart TD I[Validated composer intent] --> R{Existing submission?} R -->|same digest| E[Return existing task] R -->|new identity| C[Capture policies, target and parameter intent] C --> A[RAM admission transaction] A --> F[Compare settings, conversation, Gateway and parameter revisions] F --> G[Create or check conversation; bind context; accept profile] G --> T[Publish task, submission and pending admission notice] T --> N[Record prompt usage and notify observers] N --> W[Wake server coordinator] W --> D[Reserve attempt when eligible] D --> X[Dispatch accepted request identity]

RAM admission requires the task, conversation, settings, native and context owners to share one runtime hub. Its fence compares relevant settings, conversation policy, Gateway and parameter revisions. Enqueue's transaction rechecks that fence, creates or validates the conversation, binds supplied context, checks whether the composer must answer an existing interaction, and captures any Task Contract context manifest. Task, submission, dependency, composer and pending-admission records publish through the task store's transaction.

Prompt-history/usage recording and observer notifications follow publication. If one fails, the already accepted task is not rolled back. RAM keeps a pending admission outbox until the queued notification is acknowledged; a later tick can retry that notification. Reusing the original client submission identity is how a caller recovers an uncertain acknowledgement.

The standalone SQL adapter shares the interface but has different boundaries. Some conversation, policy and attachment preparation occurs before the task-store enqueue transaction. A failure is therefore not a promise that every preparation side effect rolled back. Do not infer the RAM cross-domain atomicity contract for standalone tooling.

RAM admission and acknowledgement sequence

sequenceDiagram participant A as Conversation-task API participant C as Admission coordinator participant H as Shared Controller transaction participant N as History and observer publishers A->>C: Validated prompt and client submission identity C->>C: Capture relevant revisions and accepted intent C->>H: Look up submission digest alt Exact accepted submission exists H-->>C: Existing task and retained context C-->>A: Same task identity else New submission C->>C: Resolve target, resources, model settings and policies C->>H: Enqueue with admission and composer callbacks H->>H: Recheck revisions, conversation and current input state H->>H: Bind context and publish profile, task, dependency and submission H->>H: Initialize parameter holds and pending admission notice H-->>C: Accepted task C->>N: Record prompt history and parameter usage C->>N: Publish queued invalidation N-->>C: Publication succeeded C->>H: Acknowledge admission outbox notice C-->>A: Accepted task and lane identity end Note over H,N: Failure after task publication leaves the task accepted

The outbox retries the queued notification, not every post-commit action. Prompt history and parameter-use recording have their own failure/retry behavior. A client recovers an uncertain response using the original submission ID. A new submission ID represents new intent and cannot serve as an acknowledgement retry. This sequence uses the shared RAM owner; the standalone SQL preparation boundary above remains different.

Task storage and retained identities

MemoryTaskStore composes lane, dependency, preparation and timing operations over TaskRecords. Nested operations reuse the current transaction; an outer write uses optimistic publication and may retry its computation. Callbacks must therefore avoid external effects. The retained caller lock is not the state authority, and _connect explicitly rejects runtime SQL access. Public reads return detached task, attempt and checkpoint models.

Creation order, queue position and request identity have different purposes. Creation order identifies accepted intent and prerequisite selection. Reordering changes only future queue positions under an exact lane-version check. A request binding identifies one attempt; retries and continuations can add attempts to the same logical task. Retained submission/request bindings prevent deleted intent from being recreated by an old HTTP retry. A binding without its task and attempt is not sufficient to project live lineage.

The RAM lane selects the first eligible task per conversation, then orders those heads by creation time. An independent task can pass a dependency-blocked predecessor. Parameter holds that have never started do not consume execution capacity. When all participating tasks are Agent tasks with explicit parallel execution enabled, the lane permits overlap; otherwise its smallest applicable execution limit wins. Native/model capacity and Gateway update admission remain separate checks. Read projections do not reserve capacity, and reserve_chat_attempt revalidates the task before publishing its attempt and current request pointers.

The store's lane view combines the latest 100 unarchived ordered tasks with queued, active and designated blocked rows, so it can contain more than 100 entries. Attempt and checkpoint list methods return the oldest bounded records, not a tail; separate latest-checkpoint methods select the newest evidence. Display-oriented compact context cannot be used as an accepted execution snapshot.

History pruning is a target, not a hard row cap. It protects active tasks, interrupted chat work, pending follow-ups and steering, lane blockers and referenced prerequisites. Eligibility is decided before deletion, so removing a descendant does not expose its ancestor for deletion during the same pass. Explicit deletion also rejects protected ownership, removes owned attempts/checkpoints and retains a task tombstone to fence late writes. Conversation collection has the separate durable acceptance and cleanup lifecycle.

Parameter holds and Runtime messages

runtime_admission.py joins task creation to the Parameter snapshot owner. Unresolved references put accepted intent in awaiting_clarification with a revisioned issue and checkpoint before any attempt exists. Attempt creation and preparation recheck the hold; changing the displayed task status alone cannot bypass it. For user controls, see Parameters and Database.

A correction requires the current issue revision and a task that has not started or been archived. The transaction replaces the accepted reference snapshot, invalidates compiler preparation and leaves the task held, queues it or cancels it. Issue identity remains stable while its revision and source-event history advance. Legacy free-form errors are projected through safe diagnostic categories; the read does not rewrite the stored record.

Usage recording occurs after task acceptance and can fail independently. The caller receives the original error for its retry policy while the task receives a best-effort structured issue. A later successful write resolves that same issue. Task checkpoints own issues created before a request; after a request exists, new issue identities belong to its journal. Existing task-owned issues can still recover. Presentation joins those histories without changing their ownership or treating a Runtime message as an Agent answer.

Reconciliation, capacity and dispatch

The coordinator reconciles when the hub revision changes or a 30-second sweep is due. Timer-driven dispatch still runs between those sweeps. It reads potentially large native evidence before taking the task queue lock, then rereads task identity under the lock so stale evidence cannot overwrite a newer attempt.

Native lifecycle truth takes precedence. A terminal run that still has a native owner keeps its lane until finalization releases ownership. answered projects as completed; confirmation/user/resource waits remain active task states. An absent native record allows only failed, cancelled or interrupted trace fallback. A completed transport trace alone cannot complete the task. Continuation children bind as eligible new attempts of the same logical task.

Each pass delivers steering, advances follow-up queues and reserves their affected conversations before considering new chat heads. Actual capacity and task-store eligibility are rechecked at reservation. A dependency failure blocks its explicit dependents; it does not automatically stop unrelated later tasks or other lanes. The store determines eligible ordering, while the worker independently limits in-flight dispatch futures to its pool size.

A task-local reservation failure leaves the head queued and allows other lanes to progress. Retry observations are bounded to 256 entries and delay subsequent attempts by 1, 2, 4, then at most 8 seconds. Only classified reasons reach those diagnostics; raw exception strings may contain accepted private data. Database, filesystem and memory failures escape the per-task handler to the watcher instead of being treated as ordinary task conflicts.

Dispatch uses the reserved request ID and accepted context. Terms, required snapshot keys and target existence are checked before request submission. If submission fails before native state exists, the worker settles only the still-current task and attempt as failed or interrupted according to submission evidence. Once native state exists, its owner controls the outcome and the coordinator wakes reconciliation. Recovery can reuse a reserved attempt missing native initialization; it does not invent a fresh identity merely because the original HTTP response was lost.

Coordinator pass and execution recovery

flowchart TD Wake[State wake or watcher interval] --> Notice[Retry pending RAM admission notices] Notice --> Evidence[Read task and native reconciliation evidence] Evidence --> Revision{Changed hub revision or thirty-second sweep?} Revision -->|Yes| Reconcile[Reconcile while fencing current task identity] Revision -->|No| Recover[Check reserved attempts without native state] Reconcile --> Recover Recover --> Resume[Resubmit only eligible retained request identities] Resume --> Clean[Remove settled dispatch futures] Clean --> Steer[Deliver retained pending steering] Steer --> Followup[Advance follow-ups under the capacity lock] Followup --> Capacity{Run slot and submission-pool room?} Capacity -->|No| Wait[Return to watcher wait] Capacity -->|Yes| Heads[Read eligible heads excluding reserved conversations and backoff] Heads --> Reserve[Recheck task eligibility and reserve an attempt] Reserve -->|Task-local conflict| Delay[Record bounded retry and consider another lane] Delay --> Capacity Reserve -->|Store or system failure| Watcher[Propagate to watcher logging and later pass] Reserve -->|Accepted| Submit[Submit saved context with retained request ID] Submit --> Capacity

The diagram separates the logical run-slot check from the eight-worker submission pool. Neither is a model endpoint slot or a Gateway resource claim. A pass may also fill the existing general task runner's available slots after considering chat heads. Follow-up dispatch and its child/projection transaction are detailed in follow-up queues.

sequenceDiagram participant C as Conversation coordinator participant T as Task and attempt store participant R as Request submission owner participant N as Native run owner C->>T: Reserve eligible attempt and request binding T-->>C: Stable attempt and request IDs C->>R: Submit accepted context using that request ID alt Native initialization has not committed Note over C,R: Recovery can resubmit this retained identity R-->>C: Preparation failure or interrupted dispatch C->>T: Settle only if the same attempt still owns current task state else Native initialization has committed R->>N: Own run execution and recovery Note over C,N: Submission exceptions now wake native-state reconciliation N-->>C: Checkpointed terminal lifecycle evidence C->>N: Check whether terminal finalization still holds ownership alt Native owner remains active C->>T: Keep existing lane ownership else Native owner has released terminal work C->>T: Project actual outcome and update attempt/task pointers end end

A crash between reservation and initialization leaves an identity to recover; an ordinary preparation failure can instead settle that attempt. Once native state exists, the coordinator cannot replace its outcome with a transport result. When there is no native state, only failed/cancelled/interrupted trace evidence supplies a fallback. A completed trace alone is insufficient. Explicit Retry reserves a new attempt of the same failed task, while recovery of an uninitialized reservation reuses the existing attempt.

Queue projection and explicit controls

Lane responses separate durable blockers from observed global capacity and transient scheduler-retry delays. The compact response uses schema version 2, one tasks_by_id mapping and lists of identities, with ACTIVITY projection applied to task records. Model usage, task timing and detail links are presentation. Up to 500 independent conversation tasks with runtime-admission/issues can also contribute messages without becoming chat-lane owners.

Editing and reordering delegate to product management and store eligibility checks. Reordering supplies the complete set of future task IDs and the observed lane version. Clear-queue removes future queued work; it does not delete saved history or claim active execution stopped.

The retained run-next compatibility route does not bypass failures: current RAM and SQL store implementations reject automatic traversal through it. An explicit start-blocked request instead names one queued task and its lane version, records the user's manual release of that task's dependency wait and wakes the coordinator. Capacity and actual execution remain scheduler decisions.

Converting a queued task into steering

steer-current converts eligible queued intent into an amendment of the active task. It rejects explicit dependencies and mismatched Gateway selection, model, mode, context, thinking choices, carry-forward and relevant accepted/live policies. The active predecessor must still be the one inspected before locking. RAM also rereads native state and deletion fences in the transaction.

Successful conversion archives the queued task as steered and records pending delivery. It does not execute the amendment inside that transaction. Delivery uses the queued task ID as the native idempotency identity; a repeat with another steering mode conflicts. The endpoint's omitted mode defaults to interrupt, while callers can explicitly choose after_response. Browser controls may choose their own explicit default, as described in the Chat tour.

Native acceptance settles delivery. A rejected amendment restores queued intent; other delivery failures leave pending state for recovery. Matching configured policies is necessary for conversion, but does not grant credentials or bypass native tool authorization.

sequenceDiagram participant U as Queue-control client participant C as Conversation coordinator participant T as Task transaction participant N as Native amendment owner U->>C: Convert queued task with a chosen steering mode C->>C: Capture active predecessor and native state C->>T: Recheck current task, predecessor, dependency and policy compatibility T->>T: Archive queued task as steered and save pending delivery T-->>C: Pending receipt C-->>U: Accepted delivery intent C->>N: Deliver prompt using task ID as submission identity alt Native accepts or already has the exact amendment N-->>C: Accepted receipt C->>T: Mark delivery completed else Native rejects the amendment N-->>C: ValueError C->>T: Mark rejected and restore eligible queued intent else Delivery raises another failure Note over C,T: Keep pending delivery for a later pass end Note over U,N: Acceptance does not mean the model has consumed the amendment

The stored steering mode participates in retry identity. RAM conversion rechecks native state and deletion fences inside the same transaction; delivery remains a separate idempotent native operation. Native processing applies accepted input at its owned boundary, as shown in the resource and amendment sequence.

Verification references

Fault-isolation fixtures exercise per-head backoff, independent-lane progress, global failure propagation, capacity projection and required accepted fields. Durable queue fixtures cover browser-independent progression, replay, retained attempts, native waits and steering identities. Composer fixtures cover visible-intent validation, accepted profiles and publication/replay boundaries. These are isolated fixture checks, not live model or Gateway workloads.

RAM task fixtures exercise runtime SQL denial, atomic rollback, duplicate submissions, checkpoint restoration and late-write tombstones. Runtime issue fixtures and parameter diagnostics cover held-task revisions, pre-inference guards, safe error projection and usage failure/recovery. Their results do not qualify external model or Gateway behavior.
